title: Memory addresses and the address-of operator
learningObjectives: Explain the language rule and its constraints.
Trace the example and predict its behaviour.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: An object's address identifies its location in the program's memory model. The unary address-of operator & produces a pointer to an object or function when the operand permits it. The %p conversion specifier prints a pointer value after conversion to void *.
understand.whyItMatters: This knowledge helps reason about C data representation, object bounds and valid memory access.
understand.analogy: Think of memory objects as labelled storage and pointers as typed references to that storage.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal pointer, lifetime and object-access rules.

explain.narrative:
An object's address identifies its location in the program's memory model. The unary address-of operator & produces a pointer to an object or function when the operand permits it. The %p conversion specifier prints a pointer value after conversion to void *.

Check the declared types, object lifetime, valid bounds and function preconditions before using the construct. Enable compiler warnings and test edge cases.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.code: Addresses connect objects to pointers and explain how functions can access caller-owned objects through pointer parameters. The exact numeric address is not a portable program property.

practise.guidedTask: address stores the address of count. The address printed by %p is implementation-dependent and may change between runs; the program should not rely on a particular value.
practise.independentTask: Identify the type of count, &count and address.
hints: Write a program that obtains an object's address and explains why the printed value should not be hard-coded or compared across executions.
Use %p with an argument converted to void *.
An address is useful only while the pointed-to object is alive and accessible.
